title: Events, conditional probability and Bayes

objectives.text: Calculate conditional probabilities using the correct conditioning denominator and distinguish independence from disjointness.
Derive a posterior from a complete partition and base rates, while keeping model assumptions and impossible evidence explicit.

blocks.markdown: A probability model has outcomes, events and assigned probabilities. An event is a set of outcomes; A∩B means both events occur, A∪B means at least one, and Aᶜ is the complement. Probabilities are nonnegative, the whole outcome space has probability 1, and disjoint event probabilities add. Counting favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes is valid only when those counted outcomes are equally likely. A list of unique scenarios is not automatically a uniform model.

For P(B)>0, $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$. Conditioning restricts attention to B and renormalizes its mass to 1. The numerator is joint mass in both events; the denominator is B, not all outcomes and not A. It follows that $P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B)$. Generally P(A|B) and P(B|A) differ. This finite-event ratio is undefined at P(B)=0; it must not silently return 0. Conditioning in continuous models on exact values needs a conditional-density framework, not this zero-denominator ratio.

blocks.source:
from fractions import Fraction
# Finite synthetic population: each row is equally likely to be selected.
rows = [("fast", True), ("fast", False), ("slow", True), ("slow", True)]
b = [row for row in rows if row[0] == "slow"]
a_and_b = [row for row in b if row[1]]
print(Fraction(len(a_and_b), len(b)))
print(Fraction(len(a_and_b), len(rows)))
print(Fraction(sum(row[1] for row in rows), len(rows)))
blocks.caption: Expected output: 1, then 1/2, then 3/4. Let A be the Boolean True flag and B be the slow group. Both slow rows have the flag, so P(A|B)=1, while P(A∩B)=1/2 and marginal P(A)=3/4. These are probabilities under the declared uniform synthetic population, not estimates validated for a live feed.

blocks.markdown: Events A and B are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. If P(B)>0, this is equivalent to P(A|B)=P(A). Disjoint events have no overlap; when both have positive probability, they are NOT independent because their joint probability 0 differs from the positive product. Independence is a model assumption or property to justify, not something proved by the word random or by observing two events on different screens. Conditioning also does not by itself establish causation.

Suppose H and Hᶜ form an exhaustive disjoint partition. Every positive signal belongs either to H∩+ or Hᶜ∩+, so $P(+)=P(+\mid H)P(H)+P(+\mid H^c)P(H^c)$. More generally sum over an EXHAUSTIVE disjoint partition, not merely several mutually exclusive events that omit some outcomes. Bayes follows by substituting that total mass into $P(H\mid +)=P(+\mid H)P(H)/P(+)$. A likelihood P(+|H) is not the posterior P(H|+).

blocks.title: A rare condition can yield many false signals

steps.text: Synthetic assumptions: P(H)=0.01, sensitivity P(+|H)=0.9 and false-positive rate P(+|Hᶜ)=0.05.
Among 10000 equally modeled cases, expect 100 H cases and 9900 non-H cases.
Expected true positives 90; false positives 495; total positives 585.
Posterior P(H|+)=90/585=2/13, about 15.38%, not 90%. These counts explain the model arithmetic, not a promised real-world frequency in one sample.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 2/13, then 18/19, then undefined conditional. Keeping the same signal rates while changing the prior changes the posterior. Fraction inputs preserve this finite rational example exactly; they do not remove uncertainty about whether the model inputs are correct.

blocks.markdown: A posterior calculation is conditional on the stated prior and signal model. If prevalence, selection, regime or signal calibration changes, the result changes. Repeating correlated signals cannot be treated as independent evidence without a justification. A high posterior is not an execution instruction to trade, diagnose or accuse someone. This lesson supplies probability arithmetic and asks you to identify assumptions, not make consequential real-world decisions from synthetic rates.

Independent transfer: make a small 2-by-2 joint probability table with nonnegative masses summing to 1. Compute both conditional directions and verify the product rule. Include a zero-probability conditioning column and reject its ratio. Then change only the prior in a Bayes model and explain which weighted masses change. Test whether an alleged partition is exhaustive before summing likelihood-weighted priors.

References: [Penn State conditional probability](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/book/export/html/485) and [Bayes theorem](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/book/export/html/495). The general partition here explicitly requires exhaustiveness and positive evidence probability. Numeric signal/population fixtures are synthetic, not empirical claims about trading or medical tests.

summary: Condition on the stated event, not its reverse. Independence differs from disjointness. Bayes combines likelihoods with base rates over an exhaustive partition, and its result remains conditional on the model.
